en: The Subāla Upaniṣad
Oṃ. That is full, this is full; from the full, the full arises. When the full is taken from the full, the full alone remains.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
First Section.
Om. Regarding this they say: "What was there at that time? To him he said: "Neither being, nor non-being, nor being-and-non-being. 1.

From that, darkness (tamas) is produced; from darkness arises the originator of the elements (bhūtādi); from the originator of the elements arises space (ākāśa); from space, air (vāyu); from air, fire (agni); from fire, water (āpaḥ); and from water, earth (pṛthivī). || 2 ||

Then that Egg came into being; having remained for the duration of a year, it divided itself into two: the earth below and the sky above, with a divine Person in the middle. That Person has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet, and a thousand arms. || 3 ||
At the forefront of all beings, he created Death—three-eyed, three-headed, three-footed, and bearing a broken axe.
Brahmā was afraid of him; he entered into Brahmā himself. He created seven mind-born sons; they, being of radiant luster, created seven mind-born Prajāpatis. || 5 ||

The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya (Kṣatriya) was made from his arms; that which is the Vaiśya was his thighs; and from his feet the Śūdra was born. The moon was born from his mind; from his eye the sun was born; from his ear came wind and breath; and from his heart all this [universe] is born.
The Second Section.

From his downward breath were born the Niṣādas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Gandharvas; from his bones the mountains; from his body hair the herbs and trees; and from his forehead Rudra was born, produced by his wrath. || 1 ||

The Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvaveda, phonetics, ritual science, grammar, etymology, prosody, astronomy, logic, inquiry, the law-books, commentaries, sub-commentaries, and all beings whatsoever—these are simply the breath of this Great Being. 2.

The golden light in which this Self dwells, encompassing all worlds—He divided Himself in two: by one half He became female, and by the other half male. Having become a god, He created the gods; having become a seer, He created the seers. He created the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Gandharvas, as well as domestic and wild animals. One became a cow, the other a bull; one a mare, the other a stallion; one a she-ass, the other a donkey; one a Viśvambharī, the other a Viśvambhara. || 3 ||

In the end, having become Vaiśvānara and having consumed all beings, he dissolves into the earth; the earth dissolves into water; water dissolves into fire; fire dissolves into air; air dissolves into space; space dissolves into the senses; the senses dissolve into the subtle elements (*tanmātra*); the subtle elements dissolve into the principle of ego (*bhūtādi*); the principle of ego dissolves into the Great One (*mahat*); the Great One dissolves into the Unmanifest (*avyakta*); the Unmanifest dissolves into the Imperishable (*akṣara*); the Imperishable dissolves into Darkness (*tamas*); and Darkness becomes one with the Supreme Deity. Beyond that, there is neither being nor non-being.
"Existence and non-existence"—this is the instruction on Nirvana; this is the instruction of the Vedas; this is the instruction of the Vedas. || 4 ||
The Third Section.

In the beginning, this world was indeed non-existent—unborn, unbecome, unsupported, without sound, without touch, without form, without taste, without smell, undecaying, neither great nor small, unborn; having realized the Self as such, the wise man does not grieve. || 1 ||

It is immeasurable, without face, without ears, without voice, and without mind; it is without brilliance, without eyes, without name, and without lineage; it is headless, handless, and footless; it is neither oily nor red; it is immeasurable, neither short nor long, neither gross nor subtle, neither small nor infinite; it is indefinable, uncovered, inconceivable, unmanifest, unenclosed, without interior and without exterior; it eats nothing whatsoever, and no one eats it. 2.

Indeed, one should accomplish this triad by means of truth, generosity, austerity, fasting, celibacy, and non-injury—these being the six limbs—and should behold it as self-control, generosity, and compassion. For him, the vital breaths do not depart; they dissolve right here. Being Brahman, he attains Brahman—he who knows thus. || 3 ||
The Fourth Section.

In the middle of the heart is a lump of red flesh, within which is that small lotus, *puṇḍarīka*, which is like a water-lily (*kumuda*) blooming in many ways; there are ten apertures of the heart, in which the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are established. || 1 ||

When he is joined with the *prāṇa*, then he sees rivers and many various cities; when he is joined with the *vyāna*, then he sees gods and sages; when he is joined with the *apāna*, then he sees yakṣas, rākṣasas, and gandharvas; when he is joined with the *udāna*, then he sees the worlds of the gods, the gods, Skanda, and Jayanta; and when he is joined with the *samāna*, then he sees the worlds of the gods and riches. When...

When it unites with Vairambha, then one sees; one sees everything—what has been seen and what has been heard, what has been experienced and what has not been experienced, the real and the unreal. || 2 ||

Now, there are these ten sets of ten channels. From each one of them, there branch out seventy-two thousand subsidiary channels. In this [state], this self sleeps and yet performs the work of sounds. Now, when he sleeps in the second enclosure, then he sees this world and the world beyond; he discerns all sounds. This is called the state of supreme serenity (*samprasāda*). The vital breath (*prāṇa*) protects the body. The channels—green, blue, yellow, red, and white—are filled with blood. 3.

Now, here within this small lotus, which is like a water-lily blooming in many ways, there are channels called *hitā*, as numerous as a hair split a thousandfold. In the space within the heart, in the supreme sheath, this divine Self sleeps; where, being asleep, it desires no desire whatsoever and sees no dream whatsoever. There, neither gods nor the worlds of the gods exist, neither sacrifices nor the performers of sacrifice, neither mother nor father, neither kinsman nor relative, neither thief nor slayer of a Brahmin—it is a body of splendor, immortal.
"This world is indeed water; this forest returns again by that very same path for the sake of waking," he said, "O Emperor. || 4 ||
Fifth Section.

The channel bestows stations upon those who occupy them; it is their bond. The eye is the internal [station], the visible object is the external element, and the sun is the presiding deity therein; the channel is their bond. He who dwells in the eye, he who dwells in the visible object, he who dwells in the sun, he who dwells in the channel, he who dwells in the vital breath, he who dwells in consciousness, he who dwells in bliss, he who dwells in the space within the heart—he who moves within all this, he is this Self. One should meditate upon that Self as undecaying, immortal, fearless, sorrowless, and infinite. || 1 ||

The ear is the internal self; that which is to be heard is the elemental; the quarters are the divine counterpart therein; and the channel is their bond. He who dwells in the ear, he who dwells in that which is to be heard, he who dwells in the quarters, he who dwells in the channel, he who dwells in the vital breath, he who dwells in discernment, he who dwells in bliss, he who dwells in the space within the heart—he who moves within all this, he is this Self. One should meditate upon that Self as undecaying, immortal, fearless, sorrowless, and infinite. || 2 ||

The nose is the internal (adhyātma); that which is to be smelled is the elemental (adhibhūta); and the earth is the divine counterpart (adhidaivata) therein; the channel (nāḍī) is their bond. He who moves within the nose, within that which is to be smelled, within the earth, within the channel, within the vital breath (prāṇa), within consciousness (vijñāna), within bliss (ānanda), within the space of the heart (hṛdyākāśa)—he who moves within all this, he is this Self (Ātman). One should meditate upon that Self as undecaying, immortal, fearless, sorrowless, and infinite. || 3 ||

The tongue is the internal self; that which is to be tasted is the elemental; Varuṇa is the presiding deity therein; and the channel is their bond. That which moves within all this—the tongue, the object to be tasted, Varuṇa, the channel, the vital breath, discernment, bliss, and the space within the heart—that is this Self. One should worship that Self as ageless, immortal, fearless, sorrowless, and infinite. 4.

The skin is the internal self (adhyātma); the object of touch (sparśayitavya) is the elemental principle (adhibhūta); and Vāyu is the divine principle therein (adhidaivata). The channel (nāḍī) is their bond. That which moves within all this—the one who is in the skin, in the object of touch, in Vāyu, in the channel, in the vital breath (prāṇa), in discernment (vijñāna), in bliss (ānanda), in the space of the heart (hṛdyākāśa)—this is the Self (Ātman). One should worship that Self, which is undecaying, immortal, fearless, sorrowless, and infinite. || 5 ||

The mind is the internal; that which is to be thought upon is the elemental; the moon is the presiding deity therein; the channel is their bond. He who moves within the mind, within that which is to be thought upon, within the moon, within the channel, within the vital breath, within discernment, within bliss, within the space of the heart—who moves within all this—he is this Self. One should worship that Self, which is undecaying, immortal, fearless, sorrowless, and infinite. 6.

The intellect is the internal self (adhyātma); that which is to be understood is the elemental (adhibhūta); Brahmā is the deity therein (adhidaivata); and the channel (nāḍī) is their bond. He who moves within all this—the intellect, the object of understanding, Brahmā, the channel, the vital breath, discernment, bliss, the space within the heart—he is this Self (Ātman). One should meditate upon that Self as undecaying, immortal, fearless, sorrowless, and infinite. || 7 ||

The ego (ahaṅkāra) is the internal self (adhyātma); that which is to be made an ego (ahaṅkartavya) is the elemental sphere (adhibhūta); Rudra is the presiding deity therein (adhidaivata); the channel (nāḍī) is their bond. He who moves within the ego, within that which is to be made an ego, within Rudra, within the channel, within the vital breath (prāṇa), within discernment (vijñāna), within bliss (ānanda), within the space of the heart (hṛdyākāśa)—he who moves within all this, he is this Self (ātman). One should worship that Self, which is undecaying, immortal, fearless, sorrowless, and infinite. 8.

The mind is the internal; that which is to be willed is the elemental; the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) therein is the divine; the channel is their bond. He who moves within all this—the mind, that which is to be willed, the Knower of the Field, the channel, the vital breath, discernment, bliss, the space within the heart—he is this Self. One should worship that Self, which is undecaying, immortal, fearless, sorrowless, and infinite. 9.

Speech is the internal self; that which is to be spoken is the elemental sphere; Agni is the deity therein; and the channel is their bond. He who moves within speech, within that which is to be spoken, within Agni, within the channel, within the vital breath, within discernment, within bliss, within the space of the heart—who moves within all this—he is this Self. One should meditate upon that Self as undecaying, immortal, fearless, sorrowless, and infinite. 10.

The hand is the internal [self] (adhyātma); that which is to be grasped is the elemental [self] (adhibhūta); Indra is the divine [self] therein (adhidaivata). The channel (nāḍī) is their bond. That which is in the hand, that which is in the object to be grasped, that which is in Indra, that which is in the channel, that which is in the vital breath (prāṇa), that which is in discernment (vijñāna), that which is in bliss (ānanda), that which is in the space within the heart (hṛdyākāśa)—he who moves within all this, he is this Self (ātman). One should worship that Self as undecaying, immortal, fearless, sorrowless, and infinite. 11.

The feet are the internal self (adhyātma); that which is to be traversed is the elemental object (adhibhūta); Viṣṇu is the presiding deity therein (adhidaivata). The channel (nāḍī) is their bond. He who moves within all this—the one in the foot, the one in that which is to be traversed, the one in Viṣṇu, the one in the channel, the one in the vital breath (prāṇa), the one in discerning knowledge (vijñāna), the one in bliss (ānanda), the one in the space of the heart (hṛdyākāśa)—he is this Self (Ātman). One should meditate upon that Self, which is undecaying, immortal, fearless, sorrowless, and infinite. 12.

The anus is the internal; that which is to be discharged is the elemental; death is the presiding deity therein; the channel is their bond. He who moves within all this—the one who is in the anus, who is in that which is to be discharged, who is in death, who is in the channel, who is in the vital breath, who is in discernment, who is in bliss, who is in the space of the heart—he is this Self. One should worship that Self, which is undecaying, immortal, fearless, sorrowless, and infinite. 13.

The generative organ is the internal self (adhyātma); that which is to be delighted is the elemental sphere (adhibhūta); Prajāpati is the divine sphere therein (adhidaivata). The channel is their bond. That which is in the generative organ, that which is in the object of delight, that which is in Prajāpati, that which is in the channel, that which is in the vital breath (prāṇa), that which is in discernment (vijñāna), that which is in bliss (ānanda), that which is in the space within the heart—that which moves within all this, he is this Self (ātman). One should worship that Self as undecaying, immortal, fearless, sorrowless, and infinite. 14.

He is the omniscient, He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of all, He is the inner controller, He is the source of all. While being worshipped with all forms of happiness, He does not partake of those various pleasures; while being worshipped through the Vedas and Shastras, He does not partake of the Vedas and Shastras. All this world is His food, yet He does not become food. Beyond this is the leader of all, the Governor, consisting of food (annamaya), the self of the vital breaths (prāṇamaya), the self of the senses (indriyātman), the self of the mind (manomaya), the self of volition (saṅkalpātman), the self of discernment (vijñānamaya), and the self of bliss (ānandamaya).

In the state of absorption there is no unity of the self; whence could there be duality? There is no mortal, whence could there be the immortal? It is not one whose consciousness is within, nor one whose consciousness is without, nor one whose consciousness is both; it is not a mass of consciousness, nor consciousness, nor even non-consciousness. There is nothing to be known that has not been known—this is the instruction on Nirvāṇa, this is the instruction of the Vedas, this is the instruction of the Vedas. || 15 ||
The Sixth Section.
In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here; these creatures are born rootless and without support. || 1 ||

The eye and that which is to be seen are Nārāyaṇa; the ear and that which is to be heard are Nārāyaṇa; the nose and that which is to be smelled are Nārāyaṇa; the tongue and that which is to be tasted are Nārāyaṇa; the skin and that which is to be touched are Nārāyaṇa; the mind and that which is to be thought are Nārāyaṇa; the intellect and that which is to be understood are Nārāyaṇa; the ego and that which is to be identified with are Nārāyaṇa; the consciousness and that which is to be perceived are Nārāyaṇa; speech and that which is to be spoken are Nārāyaṇa; and the two hands and that which is to be grasped are Nārāyaṇa.

Nārāyaṇa is the feet and that which is to be walked upon; Nārāyaṇa is the anus and that which is to be discharged; Nārāyaṇa is the generative organ and that which is to be delighted; Nārāyaṇa is the Ordainer, the Disposer, the Maker, and the Transformer—the one divine God, Nārāyaṇa. || 2 ||

The Ādityas, Rudras, Maruts, Vasus, and the two Aśvins; the Ṛg-verses, Yajus-formulas, and Sāman-chants; the mantra, the fire, the clarified butter offering—all these have their origin and source in Nārāyaṇa. The divine, singular God is Nārāyaṇa alone. || 3 ||
Nārāyaṇa is mother, father, brother, dwelling, refuge, friend, and goal.
Virāj, Sudarśanā, Ajitā, Somyā, Amoghā, Kumārī, Amṛtā, Satyā, Madhyamā, Anāsīrā, Śiśutā, Sūrā, Sūryā, Bhāsvarā, and Avijñeyā—these are the divine names of the channels (nāḍīs). || 5 ||

He roars, he sings, he blows, he rains; he is Varuṇa, Aryaman, the Moon, Time, Kali, Dhātṛ, Brahmā, Prajāpati, and Maghavat; he is the days and half-days, the moments (kalās) and the cosmic cycles (kalpas); and above all, he is the quarters of space—everything is Nārāyaṇa.

The Person alone is all this—whatever has been and whatever is to be. Moreover, he is the Lord of immortality, that which grows by means of food. The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye extended in the sky. The inspired poets, praising and ever awake, kindle that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. This is the instruction on Nirvāṇa; this is the instruction of the Vedas; this is the instruction of the Vedas. 7.
The Seventh Section.

The unborn, one, eternal is placed within the body in the secret cave; he whose body is the earth, who moves within the earth, whom the earth does not know; whose body is the waters, who moves within the waters, whom the waters do not know; whose body is fire, who moves within fire, whom fire does not know; whose body is air, who moves within air, whom air does not know.

He whose body is space, who moves within space, whom space does not know; whose body is the mind, who moves within the mind, whom the mind does not know; whose body is the intellect, who moves within the intellect, whom the intellect does not know; whose body is the ego, who moves within the ego, whom the ego does not know; whose body is the consciousness, who moves within the consciousness, whom the consciousness does not know.

He whose body is the Unmanifest, who moves within the Unmanifest, whom the Unmanifest does not know; whose body is the Imperishable, who moves within the Imperishable, whom the Imperishable does not know; whose body is Death, who moves within Death, whom Death does not know—he is this one Inner Self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the sole God, Nārāyaṇa. || 1 ||

He gave this knowledge to Apāntaratamas; Apāntaratamas gave it to Brahmā; Brahmā gave it to Ghorāṅgiras; Ghorāṅgiras gave it to Raikva; Raikva gave it to Rāma; and Rāma gave it to all beings. Thus ends the instruction on Nirvāṇa, thus ends the instruction of the Vedas—thus ends the instruction of the Vedas. || 2 ||
The Eighth Section.

This very Self, pure, is placed within the cave of the interior of the body. Amidst the midst of the body, which is strewn with fat, flesh, and moisture, utterly corrupted, resembling a painted wall, comparable to a city of the Gandharvas, as pithless as the core of a plantain tree, and as flickering as a bubble of water—therein the wise behold the Self that has emerged, whose form is inconceivable, divine, a god, unattached, pure, a mass of splendor, formless, the Lord of all, unthinkable, bodiless, placed in the cave, immortal, resplendent, and blissful;
by that [Self], they do not see [the world] at the time of dissolution. || 1 ||
The Ninth Section.

Then Raikva asked him: "Venerable sir, into what do all these things set? He said to him: "They set into the eye itself; that which sets in the eye sets in the visible. That which sets in the visible sets in the sun. That which sets in the sun sets in Virāj. That which sets in Virāj sets in the vital breath. That which sets in the vital breath sets in consciousness. That which sets in consciousness sets in bliss."
"He attains the fourth state itself; he who sets in the fourth state itself attains that which is immortal, fearless, sorrowless, infinite, and seedless," so he said.

"He attains the ear itself—he who sets in the ear; he attains what is to be heard—he who sets in what is to be heard; he attains the quarters—he who sets in the quarters; he attains Sudarśanā herself—he who sets in Sudarśanā; he attains the downward breath—he who sets in the downward breath; he attains discernment—he who sets in discernment. He attains that which is immortal, fearless, sorrowless, infinite, and seedless," so he said.

"He who sets in non-existence alone reaches non-existence; he who sets in the nose alone reaches the object of smell; he who sets in the earth alone reaches the earth; he who sets in what is conquered alone reaches what is conquered; he who sets in the diffused breath (*vyāna*) alone reaches the diffused breath; he who sets in consciousness alone reaches that which is immortal, fearless, sorrowless, infinite, and seedless," so he said.

"He reaches the tongue itself—he who sets in the tongue; he reaches that which is to be tasted—he who sets in that which is to be tasted; he reaches Varuṇa himself—he who sets in Varuṇa; he reaches the Saumya [channel] itself—he who sets in the Saumya; he reaches the udāna breath itself—he who sets in the udāna; he reaches discernment itself. He reaches that which is immortal, fearless, sorrowless, infinite, and seedless," so he said. || 4 ||

"He who sets in the skin reaches only the skin; he who sets in what is to be touched reaches only what is to be touched; he who sets in the wind reaches only the wind; he who sets in the *modhā* reaches only the *modhā*; he who sets in the *samāna* reaches only the *samāna*; he who sets in consciousness (*vijñāna*) reaches that which is immortal, fearless, sorrowless, infinite, and seedless," so he said.

"He who sets in speech reaches speech itself; he who sets in what is to be spoken reaches what is to be spoken; he who sets in fire reaches fire itself; he who sets in a youth reaches the youth itself; he who sets in Vairambha reaches Vairambha itself; he who sets in consciousness reaches consciousness itself—and that is the immortal, the fearless, the sorrowless, the infinite, and the seedless," so he said.

"He who sets in the hand reaches the hand; he who sets in what is to be taken reaches what is to be taken; he who sets in Indra reaches Indra; he who sets in the immortal reaches the immortal; he who sets in the principal reaches the principal; he who sets in consciousness reaches that which is immortal, fearless, sorrowless, infinite, and seedless"—thus he said.

"He who reaches the foot indeed reaches the foot; he who reaches the foot indeed reaches its setting. He who reaches what is to be reached indeed reaches what is to be reached; he who reaches what is to be reached indeed reaches its setting. He who reaches Viṣṇu indeed reaches Viṣṇu; he who reaches Viṣṇu indeed reaches its setting. He who reaches Truth indeed reaches Truth; he who reaches Truth indeed reaches its setting. He who reaches the Inner Controller indeed reaches the Inner Controller; he who reaches the Inner Controller indeed reaches its setting. He who reaches Consciousness indeed reaches that which is immortal, fearless, sorrowless, infinite, and seedless—thus he spoke. (8)

"He who sets in the anus reaches only the anus; he who sets in what is to be discharged reaches only what is to be discharged; he who sets in death reaches only death; he who sets in the middle [channel] reaches only the middle; he who sets in the wind reaches only the wind; he who sets in consciousness reaches only that which is immortal, fearless, sorrowless, infinite, and seedless," so he said.

"He who sets in the organ of generation reaches the organ of generation itself; he who sets in that which is to be delighted reaches that which is to be delighted; he who sets in Prajāpati reaches Prajāpati himself; he who sets in Nāsīrā reaches Nāsīrā herself; he who sets in the youth reaches the youth himself; he who sets in consciousness reaches consciousness itself—and that is the immortal, the fearless, the sorrowless, the infinite, and the seedless," so he said.

"He who reaches the mind alone, he reaches that which sets in the mind; he who reaches what is to be thought of alone, he reaches that which sets in what is to be thought of; he who reaches the moon alone, he reaches that which sets in the moon; he who reaches the child alone, he reaches that which sets in the child; he who reaches the hawk alone, he reaches that which sets in the hawk; he who reaches discernment alone—he reaches that which is immortal, fearless, sorrowless, infinite, and seedless," so he said.

"He who sets out for intelligence alone reaches intelligence; he who sets out for that which is to be known reaches that which is to be known; he who sets out for Brahman reaches Brahman; he who sets out for the sun reaches the sun; he who sets out for Kṛṣṇa reaches Kṛṣṇa; he who sets out for consciousness alone reaches that which is immortal, fearless, sorrowless, infinite, and seedless," so he said.

"He who sets aside the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) reaches the ego-sense; he who sets aside that which is to be performed by the ego-sense reaches that which is to be performed by the ego-sense; he who sets aside Rudra reaches Rudra; he who sets aside Asura reaches Asura; he who sets aside Śveta reaches Śveta; he who sets aside consciousness (vijñāna) reaches that which is immortal, fearless, sorrowless, infinite, and seedless"—thus he said. 13.

He who reaches the mind alone reaches the setting of the mind; he who reaches that which is to be thought reaches the setting of that which is to be thought; he who reaches the Knower of the Field reaches the setting of the Knower of the Field; he who reaches the Radiant One reaches the setting of the Radiant One; he who reaches the Dragon reaches the setting of the Dragon; he who reaches consciousness reaches the setting of consciousness; he who reaches bliss reaches the setting of bliss; he who reaches the Fourth reaches the setting of the Fourth—that is the immortal, fearless, sorrowless, and infinite.
"He indeed attains that which is seedless, immortal, fearless, sorrowless, and infinite; he attains that very seedless state," so he said.

He who knows it thus as seedless becomes indeed seedless; he is not born, he does not die, he is not deluded, he is not divided, he is not burned, he is not cut, he does not tremble, and he is not provoked. They call this Self the "all-consuming fire. || 15 ||

The Self is not obtained even by hundreds of expositions, nor by great learning, nor by relying on intellectual knowledge, nor by intelligence, nor by the Vedas, nor by sacrifices, nor by fierce austerities, nor by Sāṃkhya, nor by Yoga, nor by the stages of life (āśramas), nor by other means. They do not perceive the Self through exposition, praise, or renunciation. Only those Brahmins who have heard [the scriptures] and are well-versed in them perceive this very Self—having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and composed; having thus beheld the Self in the self alone, he becomes the Self of all, he who knows thus. 16.
Tenth Section.

Then Raikva asked him: "Venerable sir, in what are all things firmly established? He replied, "In the worlds of Rasātala. [Raikva asked: "In what are the worlds of Rasātala woven like warp and woof? He replied, "In the worlds of Bhūr. [Raikva asked: "In what are the worlds of Bhūr woven like warp and woof? He replied, "In the worlds of Bhuvar. [Raikva asked: "In what are the worlds of Bhuvar woven like warp and woof? He replied, "In the worlds of Suvar. [Raikva asked: "In what are the worlds of Suvar woven like warp and woof? He replied, "In the worlds of Mahar."

"In what are the Maharlokas woven back and forth? "In the Janalokas," he said. "In what are the Janalokas woven back and forth? "In the Tapaslokas," he said. "In what are the Tapaslokas woven back and forth? "In the Satyalokas," he said. "In what are the Satyalokas woven back and forth? "In the Prajapatilokas," he said. "In what are the Prajapatilokas woven back and forth? "In the Brahmalokas," he said.
"In what are the worlds of Brahmā woven to and fro? "In the Self, which is Brahman, all worlds are woven to and fro like jewels," he said. || 1 ||

Thus, he who knows these worlds as established within himself becomes the Self alone; this is the instruction on liberation, this is the instruction of the Veda—this is the instruction of the Veda. 2.
Eleventh Section.
Then Raikva questioned him: "Venerable sir, when this mass of consciousness departs, by what means and which station does it leave behind as it departs? To him he said:

In the center of the heart is a lump of red flesh; within that is the *dahara* lotus, which, like a water-lily (*kumuda*), blooms in many ways. In its center is the ocean, and in the middle of the ocean is a sheath (*kośa*). Within that sheath are four channels: *Ramā*, *Aramā*, *Icchā*, and *Apunarbhavā*. There, *Ramā* leads by means of merit to the world of merit, while *Aramā* leads by means of sin to the world of sin. By *Icchā*, one attains whatever one remembers. By *Apunarbhavā*, one pierces the sheath; having pierced the sheath, [one reaches] the skull-cap.

It pierces the skull; having pierced the earth, it pierces the waters; having pierced the waters, it pierces fire; having pierced fire, it pierces air; having pierced air, it pierces space; having pierced space, it pierces the mind; having pierced the mind, it pierces the *bhūtādi*; having pierced the *bhūtādi*, it pierces the Great One (*mahat*); having pierced the Great One, it pierces the Unmanifest (*avyakta*); having pierced the Unmanifest, it pierces the Imperishable (*akṣara*); and having pierced the Imperishable, it pierces Death.

Death indeed becomes one with the Supreme Deity; beyond that, there is neither being nor non-being, neither being-and-non-being nor neither-being-nor-non-being—this is the instruction on Nirvāṇa, this is the instruction of the Vedas, this is the instruction of the Vedas. || 1 ||
Twelfth Section.

Oṃ. Food that has come from Nārāyaṇa—cooked in the world of Brahmā, cooked again in the great dissolution, cooked again in the sun, cooked again as raw flesh, cooked again until it is moist with a net-like membrane, stale, pure, consisting of food, unasked for, and not prepared specifically for him—he should eat this; he should not beg anything from anyone. 1.
The Thirteenth Section.

One should remain with the nature of a child—unattached and blameless. Through silence and wisdom, by means of being free from all undertakings, one may attain the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*). Prajāpati spoke this conclusion: "Having known the Great State, one should dwell at the foot of a tree, poorly clad, without companion, alone, established in *samādhi*, desiring the Self, having attained all desires, free from desire, and with all cravings worn away. Having recognized the forms of death in the elephant, the lion, the gadfly, the mosquito, the mongoose, the serpent, the *rākṣasa*, and the *gandharva*, one does not fear anything from anywhere. Like a tree...

Even while being cut, one should remain firm; one should not become angry, nor should one tremble. Even while being cut, one should remain firm like a lotus; one should not become angry, nor should one tremble. Even while being cut, one should remain firm like space; one should not become angry, nor should one tremble. One should remain firm through truth; this Self is Truth. || 1 ||

Earth is the heart of all odors; water is the heart of all tastes; fire is the heart of all forms; wind is the heart of all touches; space is the heart of all sounds; the unmanifest is the heart of all motions; death is the heart of all beings. Death, indeed, becomes one with the highest deity; beyond that is neither being nor non-being, nor both being and non-being—this is the instruction on Nirvāṇa, this is the instruction of the Vedas, this is the instruction of the Vedas. || 2 ||
The Fourteenth Section.

Oṃ. Earth is food; water is the eater of food. Water is food; light is the eater of food. Light is food; air is the eater of food. Air is food; space is the eater of food. Space is food; the sense organs are the eaters of food. The sense organs are food; the mind is the eater of food. The mind is food; the intellect is the eater of food. The intellect is food; the unmanifest is the eater of food. The unmanifest is food; the Imperishable is the eater of food. The Imperishable is food; Death is the eater of food. Death, indeed, becomes one with the Supreme Deity. Beyond that is neither being nor non-being, nor both being and non-being. This is the instruction on Nirvāṇa; this is the instruction of the Vedas; this is the instruction of the Vedas. 1.
Fifteenth Section.

Then Raikva asked him: "Venerable sir, when this mass of consciousness departs, by what means and which station does it burn? To him he said: "When this mass of consciousness departs, it burns the Prāṇa, the Apāna, the Vyāna, the Udāna, and the Samāna; it burns Vairambha, Mukhya, Antaryāma, Prabhañjana, Kumāra, Śyena, Śveta, Kṛṣṇa, and Nāga; it burns earth, water, fire, air, and ether; and it burns the waking state, the dreaming state, the deep sleep state, and the fourth state (turīya) of the great ones."

It burns this world and the other world; it burns the world and the non-world; it burns dharma and adharma; it burns that which is without sun, without bounds, and without light; beyond that, it burns the Great One; it burns the Unmanifest; it burns the Imperishable; it burns Death. Indeed, O God, Death becomes one with the Supreme. Beyond that, there is neither being nor non-being, nor being-and-non-being. This is the instruction on Nirvāṇa; this is the instruction of the Vedas; this is the instruction of the Vedas. || 1 ||
The Sixteenth Section.

This *Brahmopaniṣad*, which contains the seed-syllables of Saubāla, must not be given to one who is not tranquil, nor to one who is not a son, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who has not stayed for a year and a night [in retreat], nor to one whose family and character are not well known; it must never be spoken [to such]. For him who has supreme devotion to the Divine, and as to the Divine, so to the Guru—for that great soul these meanings thus explained become manifest. This is the instruction on Nirvāṇa; this is the instruction of the Vedas; this is the instruction of the Vedas. || 1 ||
Oṃ. That is fullness; this is fullness. From fullness, fullness arises. When fullness is taken from fullness, only fullness remains.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
Thus ends the Subāla Upaniṣad.
